text.brief: In the days after June 4, 1989, a worker named Xiao Bin described the killings to an ABC News crew in Beijing.
text.record: State television rebroadcast his interview with a number for citizens to call, and two women reported him within hours ([Amnesty International, China: Preliminary report on repression after 4 June 1989 (ASA 17/09/90)](https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/asa170091990en.pdf); [Human Rights Watch / Asia Watch: Detained in China and Tibet, update](https://www.hrw.org/reports/pdfs/c/china/china945.pdf)). He appeared on television under arrest and recanted. A court sentenced him to ten years ([Amnesty International, ASA 17/09/90](https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/asa170091990en.pdf)). On June 13 the Ministry of Public Security issued a wanted list of 21 student leaders, and state television showed their photographs for days ([Amnesty International, ASA 17/09/90](https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/asa170091990en.pdf)).
text.reading: Foreign cameras gave the world its record of the massacre and gave the police their identifications. The asymmetry ran one way, because the network that aired a witness could not protect him once the Party turned his face into evidence.
text.gapText: Data Architecture. Newsrooms treated a witness's face as content and had no rule for what a hostile state could do with it.
text.fix: Protect sources in the edit as well as in the notebook, and obscure the faces of witnesses who remain within the state's reach.
